entries: Record OBD-II codes and compare CAN bus observations with OEM service manuals. A trained technician may use a multimeter or oscilloscope under the appropriate procedure. ASE credentials include A1–A8, L1 advanced engine performance and L3 hybrid/EV. EPA Section 609 applies to covered motor-vehicle air-conditioning service.

Diagnosis and inspection | Give the judgment a basis | Check key components against the checklist, measure with diagnostic equipment and gauges, determine the fault scope against manufacturer specifications, and record the measured values and the basis for judgments.

Repair and overhaul | Keep the work reliable | Disassemble and assemble per procedure and protect surrounding components, inspect for wear before repairing or replacing components, assemble and fill to specification, and avoid substituting parts replacement for diagnosis.

Testing and adjustment | Make the result reviewable | Test and adjust repaired systems to manufacturer performance specifications, describe anomalies and deviations, and add diagnosis and review when necessary.

Delivery and records | Make the process traceable | Record the symptoms and inspection and measurements and replaced parts and test results, and explain to the customer what has been handled and what remains pending, along with the costs.

Collaboration and authorization | Make responsibility attributable | Coordinate with the front desk and supervisors and parts management; when safety parts, emissions, high-voltage systems, airbags, and refrigerant handling are involved, follow the authorized process and report open items honestly.

paragraphs: Main equipment and tools | Lifts and support equipment, hand and power tools and grinders, micrometers and calipers and gauges, diagnostic scanners and infrared engine analyzers and compression gauges, air conditioning refrigerant recovery and charging equipment, and personal protection (safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection, safety shoes, respiratory protection). Task rhythm | 52% work more than 40 hours per week; 49% perform repetitive motions continuously or almost continuously, 43% stand continuously or almost continuously, 40% bend or twist continuously or almost continuously, 35% kneel, squat, bend, or crawl more than half the time, 35% walk or run more than half the time, and 36% are in confined work spaces or awkward positions at least once a week. Collaboration | Work with vehicle owners and front desk reception, workshop supervisors, and parts and inventory management personnel; 44% spend most of their time in contact with others, 38% consider cooperation with the work group or team extremely important, and 27% consider coordinating or leading others extremely important. Competition and pressure | 36% consider the consequences of errors extremely serious, 46% consider their decisions very important to colleague or company results, 42% have a lot of decision freedom, 36% have some freedom over tasks and priorities and goals, and 56% need to make decisions every day. Records and review | Symptoms and inspection and measurements and judgments and replaced parts and test results need to be traceable; 46% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, and 26% consider repeating the same task extremely important. Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the basic skills are mainly critical thinking, active listening, monitoring, active learning, and speaking; the cross-functional skills include repairing, troubleshooting, equipment maintenance, operation monitoring, complex problem solving, installation, operation and control, quality control analysis, equipment selection, judgment and decision making, systems analysis, systems evaluation, and time management; knowledge is mainly mechanical, engineering and technology, computers and electronics, customer and personal service, English language, and mathematics; abilities include deductive reasoning, near vision, problem sensitivity, finger and manual dexterity, control precision, inductive reasoning, arm-hand steadiness, information ordering, visualization, and multi-limb coordination (the details publish Importance, not frequency). Entry and authorization | Education does not equal work authorization, and industry certification does not mean you can handle high-voltage systems and airbags and safety parts in any setting; work must follow institutional processes and the applicable standards. Industry and employers | The O*NET industry distribution is retail trade 43%, other services 31%, and other industries 26%; common employers are brand-authorized service centers, general auto repair shops, chain quick-repair shops, accident vehicle repair centers, and new energy specialty shops. Supplementary boundaries | The O*NET new-hire education requirement survey is 32% postsecondary certificate, 30% below high school, and 26% high school or equivalent, which is not the incumbent composition. Zone3/SVP6.0 to <7.0 is an occupational preparation description, usually one to two years of training, not a fixed threshold for every position. The BLS EP typical entry is a postsecondary nondegree award, related experience None, and short-term on-the-job training; the OOH notes that those who have taken related courses may need shorter training, that untrained workers start as assistants or in maintenance positions with longer mentoring, and that a paid apprenticeship pathway is also available; the definitions cannot substitute for one another. U.S. ASE A1–A9 professional certification requires passing the corresponding examination and meeting 2 years of full-time equivalent related hands-on experience; Eligible study or a co-op can count toward the experience requirement under ASE rules. Check the credit for the program; substitutions cannot be combined. Most tests may be taken before meeting the experience requirement, which must be met before certification. L1–L4 is 3 years and G1 is 1 year; automotive Master requires A1–A8 all to be certified, A9 is not required, and the relevant certifications are maintained every 5 years. This is not a uniform practical examination or a whole-vehicle work permit. It applies only to the corresponding U.S. The OSHA industry hazard PDF contains 2011—2016 NAICS8111 data, with 108 deaths and about 22,200 nonfatal injuries and illnesses in 2016, covering the automotive repair and maintenance industry, which is not the current incidence rate for this occupation; it lists commonly cited 1910.132/133 and other provisions but not 1910.138, so it cannot be used to claim that all PPE regulations or per-model stop and recovery steps have been obtained.
